draft.title: Evaluating literary style
card: Style is the way an author writes. It includes sentence rhythm, imagery (language that creates pictures in the mind) and voice (the personality that seems to speak).
To evaluate style, ask how well these features suit the text's purpose. A chase scene may use short, quick sentences to build tension.
Also ask how well the style appeals to its readers. A story for young children may use playful sounds and simple images.
A judgement needs a reason. Name a feature, say what it does, then say whether it works for the purpose and the readers.
draft.remember: A style is judged by how well its features fit the purpose and the readers.

a.q: Which comment best evaluates an author's style?
opts: The short, sharp sentences suit the tense chase scene
The author uses short sentences in the chase scene
The chase scene is the most exciting part of the story
The author writes in a style that many people like
a.why: This comment names a feature and judges how well it suits the purpose of the scene. The second option only names a feature and does not say how well it works.
a.clue: Look for the comment that names a feature and judges how well it works.

b.q: A writer tells a mystery for teenagers in the voice of a friendly narrator who speaks directly to the reader. Which judgement is best supported?
opts: The chatty voice draws teen readers in and suits the mystery
The narrator speaks to the reader, so the story is a mystery
The chatty voice is always the best choice for any mystery
The story is a mystery, so the voice is not very important
b.why: The first option links the voice to the readers and to the purpose of the story. The second only describes the voice and does not judge it. The third claims one style is always best, which the card does not support.
b.clue: A judgement links a feature to purpose and readers.

a.best: The short, sharp sentences suit the tense chase scene

b.best: The chatty voice draws teen readers in and suits the mystery

problems.detail: Why (a) names options by position ('The second option only names a feature'). The options are shown in random order, so a student may match this to the wrong option. In the order shown, the second option is the right answer.

Why (b) names options by position, which breaks when the options are shuffled. It also says 'the second only describes the voice and does not judge it', but no option only describes the voice. It does not explain the real distractors, such as 'The narrator speaks to the reader, so the story is a mystery'.
A distractor uses 'always' ('always the best choice for any mystery'). It is a deliberate wrong answer, but it is flagged under the absolute-word rule.

opts: The short, sharp sentences suit the tense chase scene

a.why: Saying the short, sharp sentences suit the tense chase names a feature and judges how well it fits the scene's purpose. Simply noting that the author uses short sentences names a feature but does not say how well it works.

b.q: A writer tells a mystery for teenagers in the voice of a friendly narrator who speaks directly to the reader. Which judgement is best supported?
opts: The chatty voice draws teen readers in and suits the mystery
The narrator speaks to the reader, so the story is a mystery
I like chatty narrators, so this style is well chosen
The story is a mystery, so the voice is not very important
b.why: Linking the chatty voice to teen readers and to the mystery judges the feature against both the readers and the purpose. Saying the narrator speaks to the reader so the story is a mystery only describes the voice and mixes it up with the type of story. A personal liking for chatty narrators gives no reason tied to the intended readers or the purpose.
b.clue: A judgement links a feature to purpose and readers.
